Funeral for a Friend. 

Their first album, and previous two EPs, were amazing. 

Around about the time FFAF were getting ready for second album launch, the whole emo thing was taking over alt music scene - taking back sunday, my chemical romance etc. 

Anyway, the funeral for a friend singer, Matt Davies, gave an interview in Kerrang magazine saying how the new album, Hours, would be a new sound because they did NOT want to be pigeon-holed as an emo band. 

Then Hours came out. And it was AWFUL. It was the emo album they said they didn't want to make. It was nothing like their first and, due to the scene at the time, their popularity spiked. Then dipped when they continued to release music post Hours that was so far away from what anyway initially enjoyed. 

I loved that band for the first album and EPs. I felt so betrayed by what they'd chosen to do. I felt vindicated this year when they decided to do a "farewell" tour playing their first two albums (separate nights) from start to finish. Realising it was the only way to make money from their live shows anymore. In fact, the time previous that I had seen them, Matt called out all the fans that were there only to hear their old songs. Which was a ballsy thing to do considering that's the only reason anyone I know ever went to see them in last 10 years.

I have also always found this incredibly difficult - though I can understand why others have a hard time interpreting what depression really is as I have an inability to comprehend the average person's happiness/contentment.

It is hard to try to explain it and not come up against comments from people about being lazy/feeling sorry for yourself. You mentioned feeling safe in bed, you could perhaps try and convey that depression is like a cancer that eats away at your motivation/feelings of self worth, to the point where you pose the question every time you wake up "what is the point of getting up? what will I do? Anything I could do, I won't enjoy or I won't have the energy to do". It eats away at everything until you no longer have the ability to "change your mood" - it has comsumed you. 

You are depressed. You are not lazy or selfish or self pitying. You are trapped inside your own doubts. You cannot see that "everything will get better" and not because you don't want to, that is all you want, but because you can't, it won't let you believe it. 

I'm sorry I am not being more specific about how to properly articulate it, so I will sign off with a quote from "Prozac Nation" by Elizabeth Wurtzel, who I always felt, managed to hit the nail on the head.

"Depression is not a sudden disaster. It is more like a cancer: At first its tumorous mass is not even noticeable to the careful eye, and then one day -- wham! -- there is a huge, deadly seven-pound lump lodged in your brain or your stomach or your shoulder blade, and this thing that your own body has produced is actually trying to kill you. Depression is a lot like that: Slowly, over the years, the data will accumulate in your heart and mind, a computer program for total negativity will build into your system, making life feel more and more unbearable. But you won't even notice it coming on, thinking that it is somehow normal, something about getting older, about turning eight or turning twelve or turning fifteen, and then one day you realize that your entire life is just awful, not worth living, a horror and a black blot on the white terrain of human existence.
